S1 and S2 are used to configure the circuit for different types of operation.
R4 varies the input to Q1 and acts as a level control preventing Q1 from reaching saturation.
R1 varies the amplitude of the information signal and acts as a modulation control.
R2 is a variable resistor and is used to change the center frequency.
D1 is a varactor diode and is in parallel with C3. R2 and R8 supply reverse biasing to D1.
Q1 is the oscillator; C3, L2, and C4 form the tank circuit.
The circuit is contained on PC130-86 and consists of an oscillator for the carrier signal and a varactor diode to change the oscillator frequency.

LESSON MENU
Let's begin the lesson on FM CIRCUIT OPERATION............................
Remember, the circuits you will use in this experiment produce low power outputs and do not have many additional circuits.
However, a home FM receiver does not need many stages of RF amplification. Unless you are extremely far away from the FM transmitting antenna, you may need additional RF amplifiers.
For example, an FM broadcasting station needs to transmit a lot of power so, several high powered RF amplifier circuits are needed.
The type and number of additional circuits in FM transmitters and receivers depends on the way the system is used.
Just like AM transmitters and receivers, FM transmitters and receivers use oscillator, amplifier, and filter circuits.
FM transmitters and receivers contain more than just a modulator and demodulator.
In this lesson, you will observe the operation of a FM transmitter and receiver circuit.
